t: E chwedyl a doeth at Uendigeituran, bot Matholwch yn adaw y llys, heb ouyn, heb ganhyat.
l: The news it-was-that came to Bendigeidfran: Matholwch's being leaving the court, without asking, without leave.
i: The news came to Bendigeidfran that Matholwch was leaving the court without asking and without leave.
n: E chwedyl a doeth 'the news came' is the abnormal sentence, the tale's ordinary narrative order: subject first, then the particle a, then the verb (doeth, third-person singular preterite of dyuot 'come'); it stresses nothing. E is a spelling of y 'the'. at Uendigeituran 'to Bendigeidfran' ← Bendigeituran, softened after at. bot Matholwch yn adaw 'Matholwch being leaving' = that Matholwch was leaving: bot 'be' introduces reported fact. heb ouyn ← gofyn 'asking', heb ganhyat ← canhyat 'leave', each softened after heb 'without'. Spelling: u = v/f (ouyn = gofyn), -t = -d (ganhyat = ganiatâd).

t: A chenadeu a aeth y ouyn idaw, paham oed hynny.
l: And messengers it-was-that went to ask of-him why was that.
i: And messengers went to ask him why this was.
n: a chenadeu ← kennadeu 'messengers', with the spirant mutation (k > ch) after a 'and'; the scribe writes the word with one n here and with nn in the next sentence. a aeth 'went': a singular verb after a plural subject, normal in the abnormal sentence. y ouyn idaw 'to ask (of) him': gofyn takes y/i 'to' of the person asked, and idaw is y conjugated, third person singular masculine. paham 'why' (pa + achaws, 'for what cause').

t: Sef kennadeu a aeth, Idic uab Anarawc, ac Eueyd Hir.
l: That-is the messengers that went: Iddig son of-Anarawg, and Efeydd Hir.
i: The messengers who went were Iddig son of Anarawg and Efeydd Hir.
n: Sef 'that is' answers an implied question (which messengers?); it is dropped in i. Idic uab Anarawc: uab ← mab 'son', softened after a personal name, as in every patronymic; -c = -g (Anarawc = Anarawg). Eueyd Hir is Efeydd Hir, 'Efeydd the Tall' (hir 'long, tall'); he is sent again below.

t: Y guyr hynny a'y godiwawd, ac a ouynyssant idaw, pa darpar oed yr eidaw, a pha achaws yd oed yn mynet e ymdeith.
l: Those men it-was-that overtook-him, and that asked of-him what intention was his, and what cause he-was going away.
i: These men overtook him and asked him what he intended, and for what reason he was going away.
n: Y guyr hynny a'y godiwawd 'those men overtook him': a'y is the relative a with the infixed object pronoun 'y 'him'; godiwawd ← goddiwes 'overtake', with the old third-person singular preterite ending -awd, singular again after a plural subject. a ouynyssant ← gofynyssant, third-person plural preterite (-yssant). pa darpar ← tarpar 'purpose, intention', softened after pa 'what'. yr eidaw 'his' (the possessive pronoun, 'that of him'). e ymdeith 'away'.

t: “Dioer,” heb ynteu, “pei ys gwypwn, ny down yma.
l: “Assuredly,” said he-for-his-part, “if I-had-known-it, I-would-not-have-come here.
i: “Indeed,” he said, “had I known it, I would not have come here.
n: Dioer 'assuredly, indeed', the tale's common oath. heb ynteu 'said he for his part': ynteu marks the change of speaker. pei ys gwypwn 'if I had known it': pei 'if' of an unreal condition; ys is the infixed object 'it', anticipating the whole matter; gwypwn is the imperfect subjunctive of gwybot 'know', first person singular. ny down 'I would not have come': down is the imperfect subjunctive of dyuot (deuwn). Both verbs of an unreal condition take this tense.

t: Cwbyl waradwyd a geueis.
l: Complete disgrace it-is-that I-got.
i: I have been utterly disgraced.
n: The object comes first and is stressed: Cwbyl waradwyd 'complete disgrace' (gwaradwyd, softened after the adjective cwbyl, which stands before its noun), then a geueis 'I got' ← keueis, first-person singular preterite of cael, softened after the particle a. cwbyl = cwbl.

t: Ac ny duc neb kyrch waeth no'r dugum ymma.
l: And no-one did-not-bring a-journey worse than-that I-brought here.
i: And no one ever made a worse journey than the one I have made here.
n: ny duc neb 'no one brought': duc is the third-person singular preterite of dwyn 'bring, carry', and dugum, its first person, closes the sentence: no'r dugum 'than (that) which I brought'. kyrch is an expedition or errand, the thing one sets out on; dwyn kyrch is 'make a journey'. waeth ← gwaeth 'worse', softened after the noun it follows.

t: A reuedawt rygyueryw a mi.”
l: And a-wonder has-befallen me.”
i: And a strange thing has befallen me.”
n: reuedawt = ryuedawt 'a wonder, a marvel' (rhyfeddod); r does not mutate after a 'and'. rygyueryw a mi 'has met with me': kyueryw is the third-person singular preterite of kyuaruot 'meet', and the particle ry makes it a perfect ('has met') and softens it, k > g. a mi 'with me'.

t: “Beth yw hynny?” heb wynt.
l: “What is that?” said they.
i: “What is that?” they said.
n: Beth 'what' (peth 'thing', softened as an interrogative). heb wynt 'said they': heb takes the pronoun after it, as heb ef, heb ynteu.

t: “Rodi Bronwen uerch Lyr ym, yn tryded prif rieni yr ynys honn, ac yn uerch y urenhin Ynys y Kedeyrn, a chyscu genthi, a gwedy hynny uy gwaradwydaw.
l: “Giving Branwen daughter of-Llŷr to-me, as third chief maiden of this island, and as daughter to the King of-the-Island of-the-Mighty, and sleeping with-her, and after that my disgracing.
i: “Branwen daughter of Llŷr was given to me, one of the three chief maidens of this island and daughter to the King of the Island of the Mighty, and I slept with her, and after that I was disgraced.
n: Bronwen: the White Book spells the name so here, once only (Evans prints bron-wen across a line end, and the second witness agrees); everywhere else it is Branwen, and the spelling is kept as written. Rodi … ym 'giving to me' = she was given to me; three verbal nouns tell the story without a finite verb. uerch Lyr 'daughter of Llŷr': Llyr softened after uerch. yn tryded prif rieni 'as third chief maiden': in the language of the triads tryded 'third' means one of a set of three; rieni is a form of rhiain 'maiden'. uy gwaradwydaw 'my disgracing': the object of a verbal noun is shown by a possessive before it. Kedeyrn is a spelling of Kedeirn 'the Mighty'.

t: A ryued oed genhyf, nat kyn rodi morwyn gystal a honno ym, y gwneit y gwaradwyd a wnelit ym.”
l: And wonder it-was with-me that not before giving a-maiden as-good as that to-me was-done the disgrace that was-done to-me.”
i: And I wondered that the insult done to me was not done before so fine a maiden was given me.”
n: ryued oed genhyf 'it was a wonder with me' = I wondered; gan 'with' gives the opinion of a person, and genhyf is gan conjugated, first person singular. nat kyn rodi … y gwneit 'that it was not before the giving … that (it) was done': nat negates the fronted phrase. gwneit and wnelit are impersonals of gwneuthur 'do', the imperfect and the imperfect subjunctive, 'was being done', 'should be done': Middle Welsh has a whole set of these subjectless forms, lost from the modern spoken language. gystal ← kystal 'as good', softened after morwyn, a feminine noun.

t: “Dioer, Arglwyd, nyt o uod y neb a uedei y llys,” heb wynt, “na neb o'e kynghor y gwnaetpwyt y gwaradwyd hwnnw yt.
l: “Assuredly, Lord, not by the will of anyone who held the court,” said they, “nor anyone of his council was-done that disgrace to-you.
i: “Indeed, Lord,” they said, “it was not by the will of anyone who held the court, nor of anyone of its council, that this insult was done you.
n: y gwnaetpwyt 'was done' is a readable slip for gwnaethpwyt (the Red Book has it with the h), the impersonal preterite of gwneuthur, kept as written; the impersonal -wyt ending (lladdwyd, gwnaethpwyd) is one of the old forms worth learning. nyt o uod 'not of the will': bod 'will, consent', softened after o. a uedei 'who held' ← medei, imperfect of medu 'hold, rule'. o'e kynghor 'of his council' (o + 'e). yt 'to you' = it.

t: A chyt bo gwaradwyd gennyt ti hynny, mwy yw gan Uendigeituran no chenyt ti, y tremic hwnnw a'r guare.”
l: And though there-be disgrace with-you you that, greater it-is with Bendigeidfran than with-you, that insult and the sport.”
i: And though this be a disgrace in your eyes, it is a greater one in Bendigeidfran's than in yours, that insult and that sport.”
n: chyt bo 'though it be': kyt 'though' (spirant after a) with bo, the present subjunctive of bot. gwaradwyd gennyt ti 'a disgrace with you' = in your estimation; gan again gives the opinion. no chenyt ti 'than with you': spirant mutation after no 'than' (gennyt). y tremic hwnnw a'r guare, 'that insult and the sport', is the subject, held back to the end; tremic is contempt shown, guare (chwarae) a game, here a cruel trick.

t: “Ie,” heb ef, “mi a tebygaf.
l: “Yes,” said he, “I it-is-that suppose.
i: “Yes,” he said, “I believe it.
n: mi a tebygaf 'I suppose (so)': tebygaf is the first-person singular present of tebygu 'think, suppose'. After the particle a it should be softened to debygaf; the scribe does not show it, as often with t. Ie 'yes', assent to what was said.

t: Ac eissoes ni eill ef uy niwaradwydaw i o hynny.”
l: And yet he-cannot un-disgrace me of that.”
i: And yet he cannot clear me of the disgrace of it.”
n: eissoes 'yet, nevertheless'. ni eill 'cannot', third-person singular present of gallu. uy niwaradwydaw i 'my un-disgracing': diwaradwydaw is di- 'un-' + gwaradwydaw 'disgrace', to take a disgrace away; after uy 'my' it takes the nasal mutation, d > n. o hynny 'of that'.

t: E gwyr hynny a ymchwelwys a'r atteb hwnnw, parth a'r lle yd oed Uendigeituran, a menegi idaw yr atteb a diwedyssei Uatholwch.
l: Those men it-was-that returned with that answer, towards the place where Bendigeidfran was, and telling to-him the answer that Matholwch had-said.
i: The men returned with that answer to where Bendigeidfran was, and told him the answer Matholwch had given.
n: a ymchwelwys 'returned', third-person singular preterite in -wys after a plural subject. parth a'r lle 'towards the place'. a menegi 'and telling': a verbal noun carries on the narrative. a diwedyssei Uatholwch 'that Matholwch had said': diwedyssei is a form of dywedyssei, the pluperfect (-ssei) of dywedut 'say', and Matholwch is softened after the verb; the Red Book has a rodassei 'had given'.

t: “Ie,” heb ynteu, “nyt oes ymwaret e uynet ef yn anygneuedus, ac nys gadwn.”
l: “Yes,” said he-for-his-part, “there-is-not help for his going he in enmity, and we-will-not-allow-it.”
i: “Yes,” he said, “there is no good in his going away in enmity, and we will not allow it.”
n: nyt oes ymwaret 'there is no help, no remedy': ymwaret is help or deliverance; the sense here, 'it will not do, it is no good', is drawn from the context. e uynet ef 'his going': e = y 'his', and mynet softened after it, with ef echoing the possessive. yn anygneuedus = yn anagneuedus 'unpeaceably, in enmity' (an- + tangneued 'peace'). nys gadwn 'we will not allow it': ny + the infixed 's 'it'; gadwn is the first-person plural present of gadu 'let'.

t: “Ie, Arglwyd,” heb wy, “anuon etwa genhadeu yn y ol.”
l: “Yes, Lord,” said they, “sending again messengers after-him.”
i: “Yes, Lord,” they said, “send messengers after him again.”
n: anuon 'sending' (anfon): a bare verbal noun used as a request. etwa 'again, still' (eto). genhadeu ← kennadeu, softened as the object of the verbal noun. yn y ol 'in his track', after him.

t: “Anuonaf,” heb ef.
l: “I-will-send,” said he.
i: “I will,” he said.
n: Anuonaf 'I will send': the first-person singular present (-af) of anuon, which also serves as a future. Welsh answers a request by repeating the verb, not with a word for 'yes'.

t: “Kyuodwch, Uanawydan uab Llyr, ac Eueyd Hir, ac Unic Glew Yscwyd, ac ewch yn y ol,” heb ef, “a menegwch idaw, ef a geif march iach am pob un o'r a lygrwyt;
l: “Rise, Manawydan son of-Llŷr, and Efeydd Hir, and Unig Glew Ysgwydd, and go after-him,” said he, “and tell to-him, he it-is-that will-get a-horse sound for every one of-those that were-spoiled;
i: “Rise, Manawydan son of Llŷr, and Efeydd Hir, and Unig Glew Ysgwydd, and go after him,” he said, “and tell him he shall have a sound horse for every one that was spoiled;
n: Kyuodwch 'rise' and ewch 'go' are second-person plural imperatives. Uanawydan ← Manawydan, softened as a person addressed. Unic Glew Yscwyd is Unig Glew Ysgwydd, 'Unig Strong Shoulder' (glew 'bold, strong', yscwyd 'shoulder'). menegwch idaw 'tell him', imperative of menegi. ef a geif 'he will get' ← keif, third-person singular present of cael, also future. o'r a lygrwyt 'of those that were spoiled': lygrwyt ← llygrwyt, the impersonal preterite (-wyt) of llygru 'spoil, damage'. The king's message runs on through the next three units as one sentence.

t: ac y gyt a hynny, ef a geif yn wynepwerth idaw llathen aryant a uo kyuref a chyhyt ac ef e hun, a chlawr eur kyflet a'y wyneb, a menegwch ydaw pa ryw wr a wnaeth hynny, a phan yw o'm anuod inheu y gwnaethpwyt hynny;
l: and together with that, he it-is-that will-get as face-price to-him a-rod of-silver that may-be as-thick and as-long as he himself, and a-plate of-gold as-broad as his face, and tell to-him what kind-of man did that, and that it-is against my will I-for-my-part was-done that;
i: and besides that he shall have, as the price of his honour, a rod of silver as thick and as long as himself, and a plate of gold as broad as his face; and tell him what manner of man did this, and that it was done against my will;
n: wynepwerth 'face-price' (wyneb 'face' + gwerth 'worth') is the payment for an insult to a man's honour, his 'face'; the silver rod and the gold plate measured to his body are the old form of such a payment. a uo 'that may be' (present subjunctive of bot). kyuref a chyhyt 'as thick and as long': kyuref is the equative of praff 'thick', kyhyt of hir 'long' (spirant mutation after a). kyflet a'y wyneb 'as broad as his face': kyflet is the equative of llydan. The second witness adds words here that neither manuscript has, and nothing is supplied. a phan yw 'and that it is': pan here means 'that', introducing what is to be told. o'm anuod inheu 'of my un-will', against my will; inheu is the emphatic 'I for my part'. y gwnaethpwyt 'was done', the impersonal preterite again, here spelled in full.

t: ac y may brawt un uam a mi a wnaeth hynny, ac nat hawd genhyf i na'e lad na'e diuetha;
l: and that it-is a-brother of-one mother with me who did that, and that it-is-not easy with-me I either his killing or his destroying;
i: and that it was a brother of mine by the same mother who did it, and that I cannot easily either kill him or do away with him;
n: y may brawt … a wnaeth 'that it is a brother … who did': y may = y mae, introducing a reported fact, and then the abnormal sentence with its subject first. un uam a mi 'of one mother with me': mam softened after un 'one', as a feminine noun is. hawd 'easy'. na'e lad na'e diuetha 'either his killing or his destroying': na … na 'neither … nor', and 'e 'his' as the object of each verbal noun; lad ← llad 'kill', softened after 'e 'his'.

t: a doet y ymwelet a mi,” heb ef, “a mi a wnaf y dangneued ar y llun y mynho e hun.”
l: and let-him-come to visit with me,” said he, “and I it-is-that will-make the peace in the form that he-may-wish himself.”
i: and let him come to see me,” he said, “and I will make peace on whatever terms he himself may wish.”
n: doet 'let him come' is the third-person singular imperative of dyuot. y ymwelet a mi 'to visit with me' (ymweled â). y dangneued 'the peace' ← tangneued, feminine, softened after the article. ar y llun 'in the shape' (llun 'form, figure'): on whatever terms. y mynho 'that he may wish', present subjunctive of mynnu; e hun 'himself'.

t: E kennadeu a aethant ar ol Matholwch, ac a uanagyssant idaw yr ymadrawd hwnnw yn garedic, ac ef a'e guerendewis.
l: The messengers it-was-that went after Matholwch, and that told to-him that speech kindly, and he it-was-that listened-to-it.
i: The messengers went after Matholwch and gave him that message in friendly words, and he listened to it.
n: a uanagyssant ← managyssant, third-person plural preterite of managu 'tell', the by-form of menegi. yr ymadrawd hwnnw 'that speech' (ymadrodd). yn garedic 'lovingly, kindly' ← karedic, softened after the adverbial yn. a'e guerendewis 'listened to it': the infixed 'e 'it' and guerendewis, third-person singular preterite of gwarandaw 'listen'.

t: “A wyr,” heb ef, “ni a gymerwn gynghor.”
l: “O men,” said he, “we it-is-that will-take counsel.”
i: “Men,” he said, “we shall take counsel.”
n: A wyr 'O men': gwyr softened after the vocative particle a. ni a gymerwn 'we will take' ← kymerwn, first-person plural present of kymryt, softened after a. gynghor ← kynghor 'counsel', softened as the object.

t: Ef a aeth yn y gynghor.
l: He it-was-that went into his council.
i: He withdrew into council with his men.
n: yn y gynghor 'into his counsel': kynghor softened after y 'his'. To go into one's council is to withdraw with one's advisers to deliberate.

t: Sef kynghor a uedylyssant: os gwrthot hynny a wnelynt, bot yn tebygach ganthunt cael kywilid a uei uwy no chael iawn a uei uwy.
l: That-is the counsel that they-thought: if refusing that they-should-do, being likelier with-them getting shame that would-be greater than getting compensation that would-be greater.
i: What they concluded was this: if they refused it, it seemed likelier to them that they would get greater shame than greater compensation.
n: Sef 'that is' introduces the content of the counsel. a uedylyssant ← medylyssant, third-person plural preterite of medylyaw 'think'. os gwrthot hynny a wnelynt 'if they should refuse that': verbal noun first, then a wnelynt, the present subjunctive (third person plural) of gwneuthur. bot yn tebygach ganthunt 'being likelier with them': bot reports what they judged; tebygach is the comparative of tebyc 'likely', and ganthunt is gan conjugated, third person plural. iawn 'compensation, redress', the legal word for amends. a uei uwy 'that would be greater': uei is the imperfect subjunctive of bot, softened after a; uwy ← mwy. The Red Book has iawn a vei gymeint 'as great a compensation'.

t: A disgynnu a wnaeth ar gymryt hynny.
l: And settling he-did on taking that.
i: And he made up his mind to accept it.
n: disgynnu a wnaeth 'alighting he did': a verbal noun, then a wnaeth, the preterite of gwneuthur, makes a past tense ('he settled'). disgynnu ar is to come down on, to settle on a decision. gymryt ← kymryt 'take, accept', softened after ar.

t: Ac y'r llys y deuthant yn dangneuedus.
l: And to the court they-came in-peace.
i: And they came back to the court in peace.
n: y'r llys 'to the court' comes first, so the verb takes the particle y, not a. deuthant is a third-person plural preterite of dyuot 'come' (doethant elsewhere). yn dangneuedus 'peaceably' ← tangneuedus, softened after the adverbial yn.

t: A chyweiraw y pebylleu a'r palleu a wnaethant udunt ar ureint kyweirdeb yneuad, a mynet y uwyta.
l: And arranging the tents and the pavilions they-did for-them after the privilege of-the-arrangement of the hall, and going to eat.
i: And the tents and pavilions were set out for them as a hall is set out, and they went to eat.
n: chyweiraw ← kyweiraw 'arrange, make ready', spirant after a. a wnaethant 'they did' closes the verbal-noun clause; its subject is the court's people. udunt 'for them' (y conjugated, third person plural). ar ureint 'in the dignity of', after the manner of: breint softened after ar. kyweirdeb 'arrangement, order'. yneuad is most simply y neuad 'the hall' written together; the Red Book has neuad without the article. y uwyta 'to eat' ← bwyta, softened after y 'to'.

t: Ac ual y dechreuyssant eisted ar dechreu y wled, yd eistedyssant yna.
l: And as they-had-begun to-sit at the beginning of-the feast, (so) they-sat then.
i: And they sat as they had sat when the feast began.
n: ual y … yd … 'as … so …'. dechreuyssant and eistedyssant are third-person plural preterites (-yssant), the first standing for 'had begun', since Middle Welsh often lets the preterite do the work of the pluperfect. y wled 'the feast' ← gwled, feminine, softened after the article. The seating is the order of the first night.

t: A dechreu ymdidan a wnaeth Matholwch a Bendigeituran.
l: And beginning conversing did Matholwch and Bendigeidfran.
i: And Matholwch and Bendigeidfran began to talk.
n: dechreu ymdidan a wnaeth 'beginning conversing did': the verbal-noun narrative again, closed by a wnaeth, singular though there are two subjects after it. ymdidan is talk, conversation; the ym- prefix is reciprocal, 'talk with one another'.

t: Ac nachaf yn ardiawc gan Uendigeituran yn ymdidan, ac yn drist, a gaei gan Uatholwch, a'y lywenyt yn wastat kyn no hynny.
l: And behold dull with Bendigeidfran in conversing, and sad, what he-got from Matholwch, and his cheer constant before that.
i: And Bendigeidfran found Matholwch dull company in talk, and sad, though until then he had always been cheerful.
n: A hard sentence to construe. yn ymdidan is what both manuscripts write (the Red Book likewise); the reading the editors print, yr ymdidan 'the conversation', is their mending, not the text. As written: nachaf 'behold' throws the scene forward; yn ardiawc … ac yn drist 'dull … and sad' describe a gaei gan Uatholwch, 'what he (Bendigeidfran) was getting from Matholwch', and yn ymdidan, 'in conversing', says in what way: Matholwch was heavy and sad in talk. ardiawc is a rare word, taken as 'slow, listless, dull'; its exact sense is uncertain. gaei ← kaei, imperfect of cael, softened after a. a'y lywenyt 'and his cheerfulness' ← llywenyt, softened after 'y 'his'. yn wastat 'constant, always'. The Red Book has a few more words in the middle that are not clear in its print.

t: A medylyaw a wnaeth bot yn athrist gan yr unben uychanet a gawssei o iawn am y gam.
l: And thinking he-did that it-was very-sad with the chieftain how-small what he-had-got of compensation for his wrong.
i: And he thought that the chieftain was downcast at how little compensation he had received for the wrong done him.
n: medylyaw a wnaeth 'thinking he did' = he thought; the subject is Bendigeidfran. bot yn athrist 'that it was very sad': athrist is trist 'sad' with the intensive a- (as in athrugar below). gan yr unben 'with the chieftain', in his mind; unben 'chieftain'. uychanet ← bychanet 'smallness, how small', an abstract noun formed from bychan with the ending -et. a gawssei 'that he had got' ← kawssei, the pluperfect (-ssei) of cael. am y gam 'for his wrong' ← cam, softened after y 'his'.

t: “A wr,” heb y Bendigeiduran, “nit wyt gystal ymdidanwr heno ac un nos.
l: “O man,” said Bendigeidfran, “you-are-not as-good a-conversationalist tonight as one night.
i: “Man,” said Bendigeidfran, “you are not so good a talker tonight as you were the other night.
n: A wr 'O man' ← gwr, softened after the vocative a. heb y Bendigeiduran: heb before a name takes y, 'said Bendigeidfran'. nit wyt 'you are not'. gystal ← kystal 'as good', softened in the predicate. ymdidanwr 'talker, companion in talk' (ymdidan + -wr 'man'). heno 'tonight'. un nos 'one night', a certain night: the night before.

t: Ac os yr bychanet genhyt ti dy iawn, ti a gehy ychwanegu yt wrth dy uynnu, ac auory talu dy ueirch yt.”
l: And if (it is) for the smallness with-you your compensation, you it-is-that will-get increasing to-you according-to your wish, and tomorrow paying your horses to-you.”
i: And if it is because your compensation seems small to you, you shall have it increased as you please, and tomorrow your horses shall be made good to you.”
n: os yr bychanet genhyt ti dy iawn 'if (it is) for the smallness, with you, of your compensation': yr = er 'for, because of', and bychanet is the abstract 'smallness' seen in the last sentence but one. ti a gehy 'you will get': gehy is a second-person singular present of cael (keffy), softened after a. ychwanegu 'adding, increasing'. wrth dy uynnu 'according to your wishing' (mynnu, softened after dy). talu dy ueirch 'paying your horses' — the horses replaced, a horse for a horse; ueirch ← meirch, softened after dy.

t: “Arglwyd,” heb ef, “Duw a dalo yt.”
l: “Lord,” said he, “God may-he-repay to-you.”
i: “Lord,” he said, “may God repay you.”
n: Duw a dalo yt 'may God repay you': dalo ← talo, the present subjunctive of talu, softened after a; the subjunctive expresses a wish. yt = it 'to you'. The same thanks recur in every branch and are always given the same English.

t: “Mi a delediwaf dy iawn heuyt yt,” heb y Bendigeituran.
l: “I it-is-that will-make-fitting your compensation also to-you,” said Bendigeidfran.
i: “And I will make your compensation finer still,” said Bendigeidfran.
n: delediwaf is a first-person singular present of a verb made from the adjective deledyw 'fitting, comely, handsome': to make fitting, to make fuller. The verb is rare and its exact sense is not certain; the next sentence shows what he means. heuyt 'also, besides'.

t: “Mi a rodaf yt peir, a chynnedyf y peir yw, y gwr a lader hediw yt, y uwrw yn y peir, ac erbyn auory y uot yn gystal ac y bu oreu, eithyr na byd llyueryd ganthaw.”
l: “I it-is-that will-give to-you a-cauldron, and the property of-the cauldron is: the man that-may-be-killed today of-yours, his throwing into the cauldron, and by tomorrow his being as-good as he-was best, except that there-will-not-be speech with-him.”
i: “I will give you a cauldron, and this is the virtue of the cauldron: if a man of yours is killed today, cast him into the cauldron, and by tomorrow he will be as well as he ever was at his best, save that he will not have the power of speech.”
n: peir 'cauldron' (pair). kynnedyf 'property, peculiar virtue': the thing a marvellous object can do. y gwr a lader 'the man that may be killed': lader is the impersonal present subjunctive (-er) of llad, softened after a. y uwrw 'his throwing' ← bwrw, softened after y 'his': throw him. erbyn auory 'by tomorrow'. y uot ← bot 'his being'. yn gystal ac y bu oreu 'as good as he was best': goreu softened in the predicate. eithyr 'except'. llyueryd 'speech, utterance': the dead come back dumb.

t: A diolwch a wnaeth ynteu hyny, a diruawr lywenyd a gymerth ynteu o'r achaws hwnnw.
l: And thanking he-did he-for-his-part for-that, and huge gladness he-took he-for-his-part from that cause.
i: And he gave thanks for it, and took great joy in it.
n: diolwch a wnaeth 'thanking he did' = he thanked. hyny is the White Book's spelling of hynny 'that' here (Evans prints it with a mark over the n, which this edition drops, as it drops all his marks). diruawr 'huge' (dirfawr, di- intensive + mawr) stands before its noun and softens it: lywenyd ← llywenyd 'joy'. a gymerth 'took' ← kymerth, third-person singular preterite of kymryt. o'r achaws hwnnw 'from that cause'.

t: A thrannoeth y talwyt y ueirych idaw, tra barhawd meirych dof.
l: And next-day were-paid his horses to-him, while lasted tame horses.
i: And the next day his horses were made good to him, as long as there were broken horses to give.
n: y talwyt 'were paid' is the impersonal preterite (-wyt) of talu: no subject is named, the horses are its object. tra barhawd 'while lasted': barhawd ← parhawd, third-person singular preterite (-awd) of parhau, softened after tra 'while'. meirych dof 'tame horses', broken to the saddle; dof does not soften after a plural noun.

t: Ac odyna y kyrchwyt ac ef kymwt arall, ac y talwyt ebolyon ydaw, yny uu gwbyl idaw y dal.
l: And from-there was-gone with him another commote, and were-paid colts to-him, until was complete to-him his payment.
i: And from there he was taken to another commote, and he was paid in colts until his payment was complete.
n: y kyrchwyt ac ef 'there was a making for (it) with him': kyrchwyt is the impersonal preterite of kyrchu 'make for', and the place gone to, kymwt arall 'another commote', follows with no preposition. A kymwt (cwmwd) is a commote, the division of a cantref. ebolyon 'colts', plural of ebawl. yny 'until'. gwbyl ← cwbyl 'complete', softened in the predicate after uu 'was'. y dal 'his payment' ← tal, softened after y 'his'.

t: Ac wrth hynny y dodet ar y kymwt hwnnw, o hynny allan, Tal Ebolyon.
l: And for that was-put on that commote, from that out, Tal Ebolyon.
i: And because of that the commote was called from then on Tal Ebolyon.
n: wrth hynny 'because of that'. y dodet 'was put': dodet is the impersonal preterite of dodi 'put', of the older kind ending -et; to 'put' a name on a place is to give it one. o hynny allan 'from then on'. Tal Ebolyon is read here as 'payment of colts' (tal 'payment'); the name is the commote of Talebolion in Anglesey, and tal also means 'front, end', so the story may be explaining a name that meant something else.

t: A'r eil nos, eisted y gyt a wnaethant.
l: And the second night, sitting together they-did.
i: And on the second night they sat together.
n: A'r eil nos 'and the second night': a time phrase, used without a preposition. eil 'second' stands before its noun. eisted y gyt a wnaethant 'sitting together they did', the verbal-noun narrative closed by a wnaethant.

t: “Arglwyd,” heb y Matholwch, “pan doeth yti y peir a rodeist ymi?”
l: “Lord,” said Matholwch, “whence came to-you the cauldron that you-gave to-me?”
i: “Lord,” said Matholwch, “where did the cauldron you gave me come from?”
n: pan doeth 'whence came': pan here is 'from where', not 'when'. yti 'to you' (itti), ymi 'to me': y conjugated, with the old i and y spellings varying. a rodeist 'that you gave', second-person singular preterite of rodi.

t: “E doeth im,” heb ef, “y gan wr a uu y'th wlat ti.
l: “It came to-me,” said he, “from a-man who was in-your country you.
i: “It came to me,” he said, “from a man who had been in your country.
n: E doeth 'it came': E = ef 'it', set before the verb as a dummy subject, the abnormal sentence in its smallest form. y gan 'from (the possession of)'. a uu 'who was' ← bu, softened after a. y'th wlat ti 'in your country': y 'in' + 'th 'your'; gwlat softened after 'th, with ti echoing it.

t: Ac ni wn na bo yno y caffo.”
l: And I-do-not-know but-that it-may-be there that he-may-have-got-it.”
i: And for all I know it was there that he got it.”
n: ni wn 'I do not know' (gwnn, soft after ni). na bo 'that it may not be', with bo the present subjunctive of bot: 'I do not know that it is not there' = it may well be there. y caffo 'that he got (it)': caffo is the present subjunctive of cael, kept in the subordinate clause because the whole is uncertain.

t: “Pwy oed hwnnw?” heb ef.
l: “Who was that?” said he.
i: “Who was he?” he said.
n: Pwy oed hwnnw 'who was that (one)?': hwnnw is the masculine 'that'.

t: “Llassar Llaes Gyfnewit,” heb ef.
l: “Llasar Llaes Gyfnewid,” said he.
i: “Llasar Llaes Gyfnewid,” he said.
n: Llassar Llaes Gyfnewit, in modern spelling Llasar Llaes Gyfnewid. llassar is a word for blue enamel or azure, and the name has been compared with an Irish one; llaes 'trailing, slack' and kyfnewit 'exchange' make an obscure epithet, and no translation of it is safe. Gyfnewit ← kyfnewit, softened after the adjective llaes.

t: “A hwnnw a doeth yma o Iwerdon, a Chymidei Kymeinuoll, y wreic, y gyt ac ef, ac a dianghyssant o'r ty hayarn yn Iwerdon pan wnaethpwyt yn wenn yn eu kylch, ac y dianghyssant odyno.
l: “And that one it-was-that came here from Ireland, and Cymidei Cymeinfoll, his wife, together with-him, and that escaped from the house of-iron in Ireland when it-was-made white around-them, and escaped from-there.
i: “He came here from Ireland, and Cymidei Cymeinfoll his wife with him; they had escaped from the iron house in Ireland when it was made white-hot about them, and got away from there.
n: a Chymidei Kymeinuoll ← Kymidei, spirant mutation after a 'and'; the name is Cymidei Cymeinfoll in modern spelling (kymeinuoll has been read as 'big-bellied', but that is uncertain). y wreic 'his wife' ← gwreic, softened after y 'his'. a dianghyssant 'that escaped', third-person plural preterite of dianc. y ty hayarn 'the iron house'. pan wnaethpwyt yn wenn 'when it was made white': wnaethpwyt, the impersonal preterite of gwneuthur, softened after pan; wenn ← gwenn, the feminine of gwynn 'white', softened after yn, as if the speaker thought of a feminine noun (ystauell 'chamber', as the story later calls it); the Red Book has yn wynnyas 'white-heat'. yn eu kylch 'around them'.

t: Ac eres gynhyf i ony wdosti dim y wrth hynny.”
l: And strange with-me I if-not you-know anything about that.”
i: And it would surprise me if you knew nothing of it.”
n: eres 'strange, a wonder' (gynhyf i 'to me', gan conjugated). ony 'if not'. wdosti = gwdost ti 'you know': gwdost, second-person singular present of gwybot, softened after ony, with ti run into it. dim 'anything'. y wrth 'about, concerning'.

t: “Gwn, Arglwyd,” heb ef, “a chymeint ac a wnn, mi a'e managaf yti.
l: “I-know, Lord,” said he, “and as-much as I-know, I it-is-that will-tell-it to-you.
i: “I do, Lord,” he said, “and as much as I know I will tell you.
n: Gwn 'I know' answers the question by repeating the verb. a chymeint ac a wnn 'and as much as that I know': spirant after a 'and' (kymeint). mi a'e managaf 'I will tell it': 'e 'it' infixed after a, and managaf, first-person singular present of managu.

t: Yn hela yd oedwn yn Iwerdon dydgueith ar benn gossed uch penn llyn oed yn Iwerdon, a Llyn y Peir y gelwit.
l: Hunting I-was in Ireland one-day on top of a-mound above a-lake that-was in Ireland, and the Lake of-the Cauldron it-was-called.
i: I was hunting in Ireland one day on top of a mound above a lake there, which was called the Lake of the Cauldron.
n: Yn hela yd oedwn 'hunting I was': a verbal-noun phrase put first for weight, then yd and the verb (first-person singular imperfect of bot). gossed is a readable slip for gorssed 'mound' (the Red Book has gorssed; Evans prints gossed clearly), kept as written: a gorsedd is a mound, often one where marvels are seen. benn ← penn 'top', softened after ar. llyn oed 'a lake (that) was': the relative is left unexpressed. a Llyn y Peir y gelwit 'and the Lake of the Cauldron it was called': gelwit is the impersonal imperfect of galw 'call'. The nested speech of the story begins here, all of it Matholwch's.

t: A mi a welwn gwr melyngoch mawr, yn dyuot o'r llyn, a pheir ar y geuyn.
l: And I it-was-that saw a-man yellow-red big, coming from the lake, and a-cauldron on his back.
i: And I saw a big red-haired man coming out of the lake with a cauldron on his back.
n: mi a welwn 'I saw', first-person singular imperfect of gwelet. gwr is not softened here, though the object of a verb normally is (wr); the scribe does not always show it. melyngoch 'yellow-red', of the hair or complexion (melyn + coch). a pheir 'and a cauldron': spirant after a. ar y geuyn 'on his back' ← keuyn, softened after y 'his'.

t: A gwr heuyt athrugar mawr, a drygweith anorles arnaw oed; a gwreic yn y ol; ac ot oed uawr ef, mwy dwyweith oed y wreic noc ef.
l: And a-man also huge big, and an-evil-look unrestrained on-him it-was; and a-woman after-him; and if he-was big, bigger twice was the woman than he.
i: He was a huge, great man besides, with a villainous look upon him; and a woman behind him; and if he was big, the woman was twice as big as he.
n: A gwr heuyt athrugar mawr … oed 'and a man also huge, big … he was': the predicate first, closed by oed at the end of the clause. athrugar 'immense, enormous' (a- + trugar). drygweith anorles is not certainly understood: drygweith is something like 'evil aspect, villainous look' (drwc 'bad'), and anorles may mean 'unrestrained' or the like; the Red Book prints the word differently. ac ot oed uawr ef 'and if he was big': ot = o 'if' before a vowel; uawr ← mawr, softened in the predicate. mwy dwyweith 'bigger twice' = twice as big.

t: A chyrchu ataf a wnaethant, a chyuarch uell im.
l: And making for-me they-did, and greeting to-me.
i: And they came up to me and greeted me.
n: chyrchu ← kyrchu 'make for', spirant after a. ataf 'to me', at conjugated. chyuarch uell 'greeting': kyuarch gwell, 'to ask better', with gwell softened after the verbal noun and written uell (the w of gw usually lost on softening, here spelled u). im 'to me'.

t: ‘Ie,’ heb y mi, ‘pa gerdet yssyd arnawch chwi?’
l: ‘Yes,’ said I, ‘what journey is-there on-you you?’
i: ‘Yes,’ said I, ‘what business are you about?’
n: heb y mi 'said I'. pa gerdet 'what travelling' ← kerdet, softened after pa: what is your errand? yssyd 'that is', the relative form of bot. arnawch chwi 'on you', ar conjugated, second person plural, with chwi echoing. A journey is 'on' a person as a duty or purpose.

t: ‘Llyna gerdet yssyd arnam ni, Arglwyd,’ heb ef: ‘y wreic honn,’ heb ef, ‘ym penn pethewnos a mis, y byd beichogi idi, a'r mab a aner yna o'r torllwyth hwnnw, ar benn y pethewnos a'r mi, y byd gwr ymlad llawn aruawc.’
l: ‘That-is the journey that-is on-us, Lord,’ said he: ‘this woman,’ said he, ‘at the end of a-fortnight and a-month, there-will-be pregnancy to-her, and the son that-may-be-born then of that litter, at the end of the fortnight and the month, there-will-be a-man of-fighting fully armed.’
i: ‘This is our business, Lord,’ he said. ‘This woman,’ he said, ‘at the end of a fortnight and a month will be brought to bed, and the son born then of that litter will be, at the end of that fortnight and month, a fighting man fully armed.’
n: Llyna 'there is, that is' (llyma 'here is' with the far demonstrative). ym penn 'at the end of' (yn + penn, the n assimilated). pethewnos 'fortnight', fifteen nights. y byd beichogi idi 'there will be pregnancy to her': in context the term is her delivery, since the son is born then; byd is the future-habitual of bot. a aner 'that may be born': aner is the impersonal present subjunctive of geni. torllwyth 'litter', a word for animals' young, chosen with intent. a'r mi is a readable slip for a'r mis 'and the month' (Evans prints ar mi; the Red Book has armis), kept as written. gwr ymlad 'a man of fighting', a warrior; llawn aruawc 'fully armed'.

t: Y kymereis inheu wyntwy arnaf, yu gossymdeithaw: y buant ulwydyn gyt a mi.
l: I-took I-for-my-part them on-me, to maintain-them: they-were a-year with me.
i: I took them on myself, to keep them; they were with me a year.
n: Y kymereis 'I took', first-person singular preterite of kymryt, with the particle y. wyntwy 'them' is the emphatic doubled pronoun. arnaf 'on me', as a charge. yu gossymdeithaw 'to maintain them': yu = y 'to' + the infixed 'u 'them'; gossymdeithaw is to keep or provide for. ulwydyn ← blwydyn 'year', softened as an adverb of time.

t: Yn y ulwydyn y keueis yn diwarauun wynt; o hynny allann y guarauunwyt im.
l: In the year I-had them without-grudge; from that out it-was-grudged to-me.
i: For the year I had them with no one's objection; after that I was grudged them.
n: Yn y ulwydyn 'in the year', the first year; blwydyn softened after the article. y keueis 'I got, I had'. yn diwarauun 'ungrudged': di- 'un-' + gwarafun 'grudge, object to'. y guarauunwyt im 'it was grudged to me': guarauunwyt is the impersonal preterite (-wyt) of gwarafun. o hynny allann 'from then on'.

t: A chyn penn y pedwyryd mis wynt eu hun yn peri eu hatcassu, ac anghynwys yn y wlat, yn gwneuthur sarahedeu, ac yn eighaw ac yn gouudyaw guyrda a gwragedda.
l: And before the end of the fourth month they themselves causing their being-hated, and unwelcome in the land, doing outrages, and molesting and vexing noblemen and noblewomen.
i: And before the end of the fourth month they had made themselves hated and unwelcome in the land, committing outrages, and molesting and harassing noblemen and noblewomen.
n: mis 'month' is supplied from the Red Book: the White Book has no word after pedwyryd 'fourth', which has nothing to count without it. The sentence has no finite verb: wynt eu hun yn peri 'they themselves causing'. eu hatcassu 'their being hated': eu 'their' puts h before a vowel; atcassu is to hate, or to make hated. anghynwys 'unwelcome, not to be borne' (an- + kynwys 'admit'). sarahedeu 'insults, outrages', plural of sarhaet. eighaw is taken as 'molest, ill-treat', a rare word; gouudyaw 'vex, afflict' (gofidio). guyrda 'noblemen'; gwragedda 'noblewomen' (the plural of gwreicda).

t: O hynny allan y dygyuores uyg kyuoeth am ym pen y erchi im ymuadeu ac wynt, a rodi dewis im, ae uyg kyuoeth ae wynt.
l: From that out rose-up my realm about my head to ask of-me renouncing with them, and giving a-choice to-me, either my realm or them.
i: From then on my realm rose up against me, demanding that I part with them, and giving me a choice: my realm or them.
n: y dygyuores 'rose up, mustered': dygyuores is the third-person singular preterite of dygyuor 'gather, rise'. uyg kyuoeth 'my realm': uyg is uy 'my' with the nasal mutation shown on the possessive (the noun would be nghyuoeth in modern spelling). am ym pen 'about my head', against me. y erchi im 'to ask of me' (erchi 'demand'). ymuadeu ac 'renounce, give up' (ymwadu â). ae … ae 'either … or'.

t: E dodeis inheu ar gynghor uy gwlat beth a wneit amdanunt.
l: I put I-for-my-part (it) to the counsel of-my country what would-be-done about-them.
i: I put it to the council of my country what should be done about them.
n: E dodeis 'I put': E is the preverbal particle (= ef), and dodeis the first-person singular preterite of dodi. inheu 'I for my part'. uy gwlat 'my country': the nasal mutation after uy is not shown (ngwlat). beth ← peth 'what', softened. a wneit 'would be done', impersonal imperfect of gwneuthur. amdanunt 'about them', am conjugated.

t: Nyd eynt wy o'y bod; nit oed reit udunt wynteu oc eu hanuod, herwyd ymlad, uynet.
l: They-would-not-go they of their will; it-was-not need for-them they against their will, by fighting, to-go.
i: They would not go of their own will, and they need not go against it, for nobody could fight them out.
n: Nyd eynt 'they would not go': eynt is the third-person plural imperfect of mynet (aent). o'y bod 'of their will': bod 'will, consent', with 'y as 'their'. nit oed reit udunt … uynet 'there was no necessity for them to go': uynet ← mynet, held back to the end. oc eu hanuod 'against their will' (oc = o 'of' before a vowel; h before a vowel after eu). herwyd ymlad 'by way of fighting': they could not be forced out, so huge were they.

t: Ac yna yn y kyuyng gynghor, y causant gwneuthur ystauell haearn oll;
l: And then in the narrow counsel, they-got making a-chamber of-iron all;
i: And then, at their wits' end, they decided to make a chamber all of iron;
n: yn y kyuyng gynghor 'in the narrow counsel', in that strait: kyuyng 'narrow' stands before its noun and softens it (kynghor > gynghor). y causant 'they got', third-person plural preterite of cael: their counsel came out with a plan. gwneuthur is not softened as the object here. ystauell 'chamber, room'; haearn oll 'all iron'. The sentence runs on through the next two units.

t: a gwedy bot y barawt yr ystauell, dyuyn a oed o of yn Iwerdon yno, o'r a oed o perchen geuel a mwrthwl,
l: and after being ready the chamber, summoning all that was of smith in Ireland there, of-all that was of owner of-tongs and hammer,
i: and when the chamber was ready, every smith in Ireland was summoned there, every man who owned tongs and hammer,
n: gwedy bot y barawt yr ystauell 'after the chamber was ready': y barawt is yn barawt (the Red Book has yn), parawt softened after the predicative yn. dyuyn 'summoning' (dyfynnu). a oed o of 'what there was of smith': of ← gof 'smith', softened after o. o'r a oed 'of all who were'. o perchen 'of owner': perchen is not softened after o here (the Red Book has oberchen). geuel 'tongs' (gefel); mwrthwl 'hammer'.

t: a pheri gossot kyuuch a chrib yr ystauell o lo, a pheri guassanaethu yn diwall o uwyt a llyn arnunt, ar y wreic, a'y gwr, a'y phlant.
l: and causing setting as-high-as the ridge of-the chamber of charcoal, and causing serving without-stint of food and drink upon-them, on the woman, and her husband, and her children.
i: and they had charcoal piled as high as the roof of the chamber, and had the woman and her husband and her children served with food and drink without stint.
n: a pheri 'and causing': peri + verbal noun is 'have (something) done'. gossot 'setting, placing'. kyuuch a 'as high as': kyuuch is the equative of uchel. chrib ← crib 'crest, ridge', the roof-ridge, spirant after a. o lo 'of charcoal' ← glo, softened after o. guassanaethu arnunt 'to serve them' (gwasanaethu ar). yn diwall 'without lack, abundantly'. llyn here is 'drink', not 'lake'. a'y phlant 'and her children': 'y 'her' brings the spirant mutation (plant > phlant), which tells you whose children they are.

t: A phan wybuwyt eu medwi wynteu, y dechreuwyt kymyscu y tan a'r glo am ben yr ystauell, a chwythu y megineu a oed wedy eu gossot yg kylch y ty, a gwr a pob dwy uegin, a dechreu chwythu y megineu yny uyd y ty yn burwen am eu penn.
l: And when was-known their being-drunk they-for-their-part, was-begun mixing the fire and the charcoal about the top of the chamber, and blowing the bellows that were after their setting around the house, and a-man with every two bellows, and beginning to-blow the bellows until is the house white-hot about their head.
i: And when it was known that they were drunk, they began to mix the fire and the charcoal over the top of the chamber, and to blow the bellows that had been set round the house, a man to every two bellows; and the bellows were blown until the house was white-hot about them.
n: wybuwyt ← gwybuwyt, the impersonal preterite of gwybot 'know', softened after pan; dechreuwyt, the impersonal preterite of dechreu 'begin'. eu medwi 'their getting drunk' (meddwi). am ben 'about the top of' ← penn, softened after am. a oed wedy eu gossot 'that were after their setting' = had been set. yg kylch 'around' (yng nghylch, the nasal shown only on yn). a gwr a pob dwy uegin 'and a man with every two bellows': megin softened after dwy. yny uyd 'until it is': a present tense, as in the pilot's ual y byd, for a vivid moment. burwen 'pure white' (pur + gwen).

t: Ac yna y bu y kynghor ganthunt hwy ymherued llawr yr ystauell; ac yd arhoes ef yny uyd y pleit haearn yn wenn.
l: And then was the counsel with-them they in-the-middle of-the floor of-the chamber; and he-waited he until is the wall of-iron white.
i: And then they held council in the middle of the chamber floor; and he waited until the iron wall was white.
n: y bu y kynghor ganthunt 'the counsel was with them' = they held a council: ganthunt is gan conjugated, third person plural. ymherued 'in the middle of' (yn + perued, with the nasal mutation). yd arhoes 'waited', third-person singular preterite of aros (arhoi). pleit 'wall, side, partition'. yny uyd again: 'until it is'.

t: Ac rac diruawr wres, y kyrchwys y bleit a'e yscwyd a'y tharaw gantaw allan, ac yn y ol ynteu y wreic.
l: And for huge heat, he-made-for the wall with his shoulder and striking-it with-him out, and after-him he-for-his-part his wife.
i: And for the great heat he charged the wall with his shoulder and burst it out, and his wife after him.
n: rac 'for, because of'. wres ← gwres 'heat', softened after diruawr 'huge'. y kyrchwys 'made for, charged', third-person singular preterite of kyrchu. y bleit ← pleit, feminine, softened after the article. a'e yscwyd 'with his shoulder'. a'y tharaw 'and striking it': 'y 'her, it' refers to the feminine pleit and brings the spirant mutation (taraw > tharaw). gantaw allan 'out with him', so that it went out before him. yn y ol ynteu y wreic 'after him his wife', with no verb.

t: A neb ny dieghis odyna namyn ef a'e wreic.
l: And no-one did-not-escape from-there except him and his wife.
i: And no one escaped from there but he and his wife.
n: neb ny dieghis 'no one escaped': Welsh doubles the negative, neb with ny; dieghis is the third-person singular preterite (-is) of dianc. odyna 'from there'. namyn 'but, except'.

t: Ac yna o'm tebygu i, Arglwyd,” heb y Matholwch wrth Uendigeiduran, “y doeth ef drwod attat ti.”
l: And then, by-my supposing I, Lord,” said Matholwch to Bendigeidfran, “he-came he across to-you.”
i: And then, as I suppose, Lord,” said Matholwch to Bendigeidfran, “he came over to you.”
n: o'm tebygu i 'by my supposing': o + 'm 'my', with the verbal noun tebygu. heb y Matholwch wrth Uendigeiduran 'said Matholwch to Bendigeidfran': wrth 'to', softening the name. drwod 'across, over' (drosodd). attat ti 'to you', at conjugated. Here Matholwch's long speech ends.

t: “Yna dioer,” heb ynteu, “y doeth yma, ac y roes y peir y minheu.”
l: “Then assuredly,” said he-for-his-part, “he-came here, and he-gave the cauldron to me.”
i: “Then indeed,” he said, “he came here, and he gave the cauldron to me.”
n: Yna … y doeth yma 'then … he came here': the time adverb first, then the verb with y. y roes 'gave', third-person singular preterite of rodi (rhoes). y minheu 'to me for my part': y 'to' with the emphatic pronoun.

t: “Pa delw, Arglwyd, yd erbynneisti wynteu?”
l: “What manner, Lord, did-you-receive them?”
i: “And how, Lord, did you receive them?”
n: Pa delw 'what form, in what way?' (delw 'image, form'), then yd and the verb. erbynneisti = erbynneist ti, the second-person singular preterite of erbyn 'receive', with ti run into it. wynteu 'them for their part'.

t: “Eu rannu ym pob lle yn y kyuoeth, ac y maent yn lluossauc, ac yn dyrchauael ym pob lle, ac yn cadarnhau y uann y bythont, o wyr ac arueu goreu a welas neb.”
l: “Their dividing in every place in the realm, and they-are numerous, and rising in every place, and fortifying the place where they-are, with men and arms the-best that anyone saw.”
i: “I dispersed them in every part of the realm, and they are many, and they are thriving everywhere, and fortifying every place they settle in with the best men and arms that anyone ever saw.”
n: Eu rannu 'their dividing': the verbal noun with eu 'their' as its object, used as a past answer without a finite verb. y maent 'they are'. yn lluossauc 'numerous' (lluosog). yn dyrchauael 'rising', prospering. cadarnhau 'strengthen, fortify'. y uann ← mann 'place', softened after the article. y bythont 'where they are (wont to be)': bythont is a third-person plural consuetudinal present of bot; the Red Book has y bont. goreu a welas neb 'the best that anyone saw': welas ← gwelas, third-person singular preterite of gwelet.
